Great on any Friday: 70mai M800 4K Dash Cam - Front+Rear, Voice Control, Parking Monitor
Why Is the Tesla Cybertruck Suddenly America's Fastest-Selling Used Pickup Truck?
66 photos
Photo: Tesla
Well, this is unexpected. Here we have an EV so commercially unsuccessful that its manufacturer announced it would discontinue production as early as next year. Yet, if you're a used car dealer in the United States, you might just want to stock up on Cybertrucks, as opposed to the always-popular Ford F-150.
According to a recent iSeeCars study, which looked at roughly 1.1 million used vehicle sales in October, the Cybertruck needed an average of just 39.1 days to find a new owner, compared to a whopping 65.5 days for the pickup truck segment as a whole. This is even more staggering when factoring in the fact that back in December of 2024, used Cybertrucks were spending roughly 75 days on dealer lots.
And no, Tesla hadn't yet announced they would be pulling the plug on the Cybertruck when the October 2026 data was first coming in. Otherwise, one could accuse people of simply rushing to get their hands on something that could one day become a collector's item. I mean, could it? I guess stranger things have happened.
So, what's so different about a used Cybertruck as opposed to a brand-new one? Aside from the pricing, of course - actually, it's not that big of a difference. Used models cost anywhere between 9% and 18% below MSRP, on average. Also, let's clarify again that we're talking about the Cybertruck becoming America's fastest-selling pickup truck, not its best-selling one. There's a considerable difference.
Here we go. I think there's an argument to be made that American buyers never really rejected the idea of the Cybertruck to begin with. Elon's politics aside, looks aside, valuation aside. I remember there being a ton of enthusiasm surrounding the Cybertruck reveal back in 2019 - which had a lot to do with its styling. People were intrigued by the notion of owning a pickup that looked more like a Hollywood movie prop than anything else.
We tend to look at depreciation as an indication of how poorly a vehicle has been received by the public, but that's not at all how it works. Besides, there are several examples of depreciation making a car genuinely competitive for the first time. And there are plenty of luxury and performance vehicles I would happily recommend purchasing second-hand, but would have a difficult time recommending at MSRP. This is well documented.
Photo: Tesla I suspect something similar is happening with the Cybertruck , even though the study doesn't tell us how much money actually exchanged hands. I've also never been entirely convinced that Tesla fully understood who their customers were in terms of buying Cybertrucks.
If you've been driving an F-150 all your life, towing your boat in the summertime, going on long road trips and so on, what would even be the point in switching to what would have been a much more expensive Tesla? And how much of what makes the Cybertruck interesting from an engineering and design standpoint would have been of any real consequence to you as a customer?
Let's switch it up and picture someone who's been driving a high-performance luxury SUV for the past 10 years and has never towed anything in their life. Now that's the type of person you're likely to get behind the wheel of a Cybertruck if you're Tesla . You think any Mercedes-AMG G 63 owners purchased their vehicles because of their off-road prowess? I doubt you'd even need both hands to count them.
There's a whole demographic of luxury car buyers for whom a vehicle's ability to generate an emotional response is more important than what that vehicle was engineered to do. The Cybertruck was always going to be right up their alley. Unfortunately for Tesla, there's no shortage of interesting cars available to people with $100,000 burning a hole in their pocket. The Cybertruck's novelty factor alone simply wasn't strong enough.
But things are very different on the used car market, where right now you could find yourself choosing between a Cybertruck and a relatively unremarkable midsize premium SUV, which can tilt the scales in favor of the former. Even I would be more inclined to put up with the Tesla's shortcomings under those circumstances.
Photo: Tesla Then there's the exclusivity factor. Had the Cybertruck sold in the hundreds of thousands, how much of what makes it a desirable proposition would have been lost in the process? We'll never know. As things stand right now, Tesla will depart the full-size pickup truck segment without ever having posed a serious threat to Detroit's Big 3. The Cybertruck is leaving with a whimper, not a bang.
In the end, it looks as though America's used car dealers are doing a way better job of selling the Cybertruck than Tesla ever has .
And come next year, if you'll want a brand-new, fully electric pickup truck, you can always call up Rivian and land yourself an R1T , unless you'd rather go for the Silverado EV/Sierra EV, or the Hummer EV Pickup.
